items.stem: Using Przybylski and Weinstein (2017) as supporting evidence, explain effects of digital technology on well-being.
items.answer: Przybylski and Weinstein (2017). Aim: to test whether the relationship between digital screen time and adolescent well-being is non-linear. Method: Over 120,000 15-year-olds in England reported their time on films, games, computers and smartphones on weekdays and weekends and completed the Warwick-Edinburgh Mental Well-Being Scale. items.stem: Using Kross et al. (2013) as supporting evidence, explain social media use and well-being.
items.answer: Kross et al. (2013). Aim: to investigate whether Facebook use predicts changes in subjective well-being over time. Method: 82 young adults in Ann Arbor, USA, were sent text messages five times a day for two weeks asking how they felt, how lonely they were and how much they had used Facebook since the last message. Findings: the more participants used Facebook at one time point, the worse they felt at the next, and the more they used it over two weeks, the more their life satisfaction declined; feeling bad did not predict later Facebook use Link: social media use and well-being.

items.stem: "Technology has improved the validity of psychological research." To what extent do you agree with this statement?
items.answer: Technology has added objective and large-scale measures, but each tool has validity limits that must be considered.

items.stem: Describe the study by Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011) and explain what it shows about cognitive offloading and the internet as transactive memory.
items.answer: Sparrow, Liu and Wegner (2011). Aim: to investigate whether expecting to have future access to information reduces memory for it. Method: Harvard students typed 40 trivia statements into a computer; half were told the computer would save them and half that they would be erased; recall of the statements, and memory for the folder where each was saved, were then tested. Findings: participants who believed the statements would be erased recalled more of them; participants remembered where information was stored better than the information itself Link: cognitive offloading and the internet as transactive memory.
